text:
Let's dive into the signs & symptoms of Parkinson's here


























Main Symptoms

Tremor




Shaking of one body part or   multiple, typically more pronounced on one side of the body

Muscle Rigidity

Stiffness in some areas or multiple areas of   the body. Most prominent in the thoracic/core region of the body

Slowness
(Bradykinesia)

Slow movements especially during   ‘off’ phase. BIG movements need to be emphasized all throughout class as much   as possible so students continue to move BIG on their home outside of class.

Postural Instability






Poor posture (hunched over, rounded   shoulders) and poor balance

Dyskinesia (this is   a drug side effect) 

Involuntary, erratic movements of   the face, arms, trunk and legs. Typically occurs as a result of peak   medication effect of levodopa. Some students do prefer to have dyskinesia  than feel off and rigid. 




Stress and cognitive multitasking seem to worsen it.   



Secondary Symptoms

Stooped Posture

Forward leaning position causes  centre   of gravity to shift. This results in greater risk of falling. Back pain and   overall body stiffness are common   symptoms.




Shuffling Gate or Freezing

Small, hesitant steps can lead to shuffling   gate. They tend to walk with their feet very close together *** Increased fall risk***



Secondary Motor Symptoms

Decreased Arm Swing

Often one side of the body is more   affected with Parkinson’s (PD) and you can notice a decreased arm swing when   the client is walking. 




Lack of facial expression

Clients often have a masked expression   because the stiffness can often be in their face as well as the rest of their   body





parkinsons-101-202-image-header-2880x884
.jpeg
Download JPEG • 86KB





Microphagia

Very small handwriting, often one   of the first signs of the disease

Difficulty getting out of bed and turning over

Stiffness is often worse in the morning so   warm up and cool down stretches are important.




NOTE: If turning   over is a main complaint please review turning over exercise so client can practice daily at home



Secondary Non-Motor Symptoms

Voice is Quiet &   Difficulty Speaking

As Parkinson’s   progresses, changes in the






 vocal cords can occur. The muscle of the vocal   cord becomes thinner and lighter. The vocal cords stop vibrating as they   should, and a gap develops between the cords. When the vocal cords do not   fully close this gap will cause the voice to be soft or hoarse.

Painful Muscle cramps

Often in the feet but can present in   different areas of the body. 




Poor sleeping   patterns, hallucinations, vivid dreams

When   sleep is disrupted, it often leads to exacerbations of symptoms. Excessive   daytime sleepiness. Hallucinations and delusions can be present as the   disease progresses typically as a result of side effects of medication.




Depression& Anxiety




A lot of people with Parkinson’s isolate   themselves from friends and family and social activities. They tend to have   increased anxiety which can exacerbate their symptoms. They can become   fearful and overwhelmed quite easily.




Cognitive Issues   & Dementia-

Some people with Parkinson's   disease (PD) experience mild to moderate cognitive impairment. To some   degree, cognitive impairment affects many people with PD. The brain changes   that lead to motor symptoms can also result in slowness in memory and   thinking. Stress, medication and depression can also contribute to these   changes.

As the disease progresses students   can start to take longer processing directions in class or not clearly   understand directions for an exercise.




Skin Problems

Oily or Scaly skin which can lead to dry skin.   As a result, some students may not be able to   go barefoot in the gym. You can recommend non-slip socks or wearing indoor   shoes if needed. 

Constipation

Is very common among PD students.   It’s important to suggest the student to speak with health care practitioners   to get on top of their digestive health as its proven to be a very important   part of the PD puzzle.






Low Blood Pressure

Low blood pressure is quite common among   people with PD. It can either be a symptom related to PD or a side effect   from the medication. It’s best to exercise caution at every station that   consists of going down to the ground and make sure there is a chair at the   station. There are many modifications to exercises that consists of going   down and back up so make sure to be aware of them. It is very important that   the students get comfortable with the ground so teaching them how to get up   and down without symptoms is very important.

text:
Hoehn & Yahr - 5 Stages of Parkinson’s- here





Two doctors named Dr. Hoehn and Dr. Yahr developed a scale that puts Parkinson’s disease into five stages. The first stage is the mildest stage of the disease and stage five is the worst stage.

The symptoms may be mild or severe or happen a lot, or not as much. Also, the time spent at each stage of the disease varies, and the skipping of stages, from Stage 1 to Stage 3, for example, is not uncommon.




Stage 1

The main symptoms - tremor, muscle stiffness,   slowness of movement and problems with posture- are only on one side of the   body. Problems with balance might also appear.

Stage 2

The disease will be on both sides of the body   now and minor symptoms like problems with swallowing, talking and something   called “facial masking” (loss of facial expression) may be noticed.

Stage 3

The same symptoms as Stage 2 are still there   but may be worse now. Problems with balance will now be noticed for the first   time. At this stage, the person with Parkinson's is still independent.

Stage 4

The person with Parkinson's will now be   getting more and more disabled and will need help with some or all activities   of daily living.

Stage 5

At this stage the person is confined to a   wheelchair or bed and needs total assistance.





What can I expect to see in a class between the different stages of Parkinson’s Disease?


Parkinson’s Disease Stages 1-5



Stage 1

    High functioning

    Possibly newly diagnosed

No   cognitive concerns

    Minimal on/off periods

    Able to make modifications on   their own

    Still in denial about disease and   not wanting others to know yet

    Competitive in class (some   competition is great to have but keep an eye out for those “weekend   warriors”)

    Heart rate should stay in the 80%   THR zone for best results

    Still working

Stage 2

    Symptoms more visible

    Posture, gait and balance can be   more affected

    More modifications will be needed

    Work becomes more stressful and   can lead to exacerbations of symptoms

    Voice can be affected, low tone

Stage 3

    Movements   are much slower

    Cognitive   impairments are noticeable

    Non-verbal   communication issues

    De-Conditioning

Stage 4

    Later Stage Parkinson’s

    Walking limitations

    Cognitive impairments

    One-on-one assistance often   required during class

Stage 5

    Wheelchair bound or possibly   bedridden depending on other symptoms

Why do an assessment, and what does one consist of?
Learn here































Assessments are necessary to observe the students balance, strengths, weaknesses and fall risk. Note: Even if the student has had an assessment by another health care practitioner you still need to complete their health assessment with them *NO EXCEPTIONS* 



What does an assessment consist of?

    Health History forms 

    Parkinsons Questionnaire

    Fullerton Advanced Balance Scale

    B4H Assessment form	

All forms MUST be filled out by the student prior to assessment and reviewed for any red flags during the assessment.

B4H Staff assigns clients to the appropriate class and not the other way around. Some students might think they are more mobile and should be in a stronger class even thought they use a cane. This is always at your discretion and needs to be brought up at the end of the assessment. 

Clients who stay with you will progress and need more assistance at some point and then a hard discussion will need to happen if they need to be put in a different class. 

You have the rights to use our documentation or you can come up with your own but B4H head office would need to authorize it first. 



Assessment Tests

    Video of the student walking the length of the gym and back 
 (This a great tool to use for before and after results)



A.Dubois initial walk
.mp4
Download MP4 • 1.76MB



    Timed up and go test (TUUG)

    Sit to stand Test

    Timed DOWN to the ground and back UP 

    Timed walking backwards 10 feet

If there are any tests you aren’t comfortable performing due to safety or lack of stability, then do not do them - Safety first! 



Possible RED flags during assessment

    High or low blood pressure- make sure it’s being monitored by their MD

Note: We have seen several students with high BP that stay committed to our program and improve their overall health which lowers their BP. This can sometimes result in experiencing low BP symptoms like light headedness and dizziness during a class. IF this occurs please make sure you tell the student to go and see their doctor as their medications may need adjusting.

    

On blood thinners- student can bruise very easily- recommendation would be to use the softest punching bags in the gym and monitor for changes




    Osteoporosis- avoid activities such as running, jumping or jerky type movements




    Cognition- If you notice that a student is having difficulty with cognitive tasks such as following instructions then they likely need to placed in a PD ¾ class. They wouldn’t be able to keep up in a high functioning class even if they are physically high functioning. 

Pre-existing injuries and/or surgeries- make sure to check in with student during assessment about any injuries to knees, hips, back that they may have left out of their health history forms

You'll begin by securing a teaching location and diving into your online training, then move into hands-on practice with current clients while you learn. Functional Portion of Class- here





































Functional Exercises are natural movements that we find ourselves doing throughout the day like squatting to sit down, reaching up high to grab something or bending down to pick something up. This is where you can focus on implementing the VIGOR acronym you are about to learn. 




Why are we focusing on these specific exercises?




Well, Did you know that your brain has the ability to change and adapt throughout a person's life? This is called Neuroplasticity. Once you start teaching our program to Seniors and people with Parkinson's you will be able to see these changes in real time. It's like the brain's way of rewiring itself in response to experiences, learning, and challenges. Just like a muscle that gets stronger when you exercise it, the brain becomes more flexible and efficient when it's "exercised" through new activities and learning.

PD Warrior Exercises- Learn here

































































GOAL- FORCE & POWER




1- Ball Throw https://youtu.be/40Py_LXA-kQ




This activity is crafted to stimulate force and power in the upper limbs, making it particularly beneficial for individuals who struggle with slow, limited movements or tremors. The exercise incorporates a balance component during the ball throw and necessitates control and coordination to successfully catch the ball in its entirety.




Precautions

BACK- If a client has back issues be sure not to arch the back when throwing and have them use more of their legs for the force. 

SHOULDER- If you have a shoulder injury you could try throwing underarm from a standing position or throwing directly down to the floor.

BALANCE- If you are concerned about balance, have a chair in front of you and have a volunteer pick up the ball when it falls.  




2- Stop & Squat https://youtu.be/10Ybc-q-AaE




The emphasis of this exercise lies in the power squat, aiming to enhance the strength of your legs and lower back, while also promoting full extension and amplitude in your arms and hands.

BIG, open hands, wrists extended, arms reaching out and chest up.




Precautions

KNEE PAIN- Start with slower squats, or half squats. You can use a wedge/pillow on the chair so the client doesn’t have to come down as low. 

BALANCE- place a chair in front of them and behind them to make them feel safe and sturdy.

SHOULDER- Change the position of the arms and have them go out to the side.




3- TAHDAHS https://youtu.be/VhULAtOM24U




This exercise is geared towards shoulder extension, stepping and BIG arm movement. There is also a balance and coordination component. 

Make sure that BOTH movements are powerful going out and coming back in. 




Precautions

Modify exercise as appropriate if there is pre-existing injury. 

BALANCE- place a chair nearby and start with one hand only






4- SCARF SNATCH https://youtu.be/kw3XHS2swTE




This exercise centers around arm swing and dynamic, forceful movements. It proves particularly effective for individuals experiencing bradykinesia as their primary symptom, coupled with challenges in dexterity or diminished arm swing. As you advance, the task's complexity can be readily heightened to further challenge your capabilities.

Do not wait for it to fall down and do not try to catch it underarm. The point of the exercise is to be fast enough to catch it overhead. 




Precautions

SHOULDER- throw underarm and bend at your elbow so you can still get some force. 

BALANCE- chair in front of the client




5- SKY REACH https://youtu.be/DjWv0vljlzw




We are focusing on trunk rotation and BIG & powerful  arm and shoulder movements. This exercise can contribute to enhancing the overall flexibility of your back, trunk, and even your shoulder joints. Begin by taking a seated position and utilize one hand to stabilize yourself by gripping onto the chair. While remaining seated, adopt a wide and supportive stance with your legs. Once you're prepared, extend your free hand diagonally down and across your body. If you're able to reach the floor on the outside of your foot, you're doing great! Gently return to an upright position. As you do so, direct your gaze upward toward your outstretched hand. This movement should generate a potent stretch across your chest, upper back, and extend into your arm and hand. Throughout this exercise, focus on embodying a sense of strength and empowerment.




Precautions




BACK- be cautious if your back is an issue. Stop at your knee if the floor is too low to reach.




6- Double 007 https://youtu.be/BeJMw-lkC9o




The primary goal of this exercise is to enhance your trunk rotation. Many individuals living with Parkinson's experience stiffness and a reduction in trunk rotation. This issue can have repercussions on various aspects such as walking, turning, and overall balance. The exercise specifically addresses these concerns, particularly when it comes to changing directions.




Precautions

BACK- important to pivot on the opposite leg and keep your hands straight to protect your back. 

Keep your eyes focused on your hands

BALANCE- Don’t hesitate to have a chair, table or something to help stabilize you if needed 




7- Over the River https://youtu.be/EM-VzOs3Xz8




This exercise is highly beneficial for enhancing your ability to synchronize BIG strides with robust arm swings. It also contributes to refining your 180-degree turns. For this activity, you'll require a clearly marked line on the floor. Ensure you elevate your knee significantly during the movement, while your arms should exhibit forceful and straight swinging motions as you reach the final position.




Precautions

KNEES- make a smaller step over the hurdle




9- Penguin Waddle https://youtu.be/Q9EWH7yaNmI




This exercise places emphasis on weight shifting and serves as an effective method for practicing stepping. It proves to be a valuable technique, especially when dealing with minor episodes of freezing while walking. Additionally, you'll find that it provides an excellent workout for your gluteal muscles!




Precautions

DIZZY- just go in one single direction or pause after each box rotation

BALANCE- You can place a chair on either side 




10- Banded Side Step https://www.youtube.com/shorts/JBC65ii_IAM




This exercise focuses on posture, coordination and upper limb resistance and is really helpful to get the muscles in your back and arms working hard. 




Precautions

SHOULDER- Keep your arms low with your hands below your shoulders




11- Box Step https://youtu.be/3fo1INxGGiI




Why focus on posture? We are working with our clients to counteract the stooped posture that develops as we age, and even more so if you have Parkinsons.

When we work on posture exercises we are strengthening the front(flexors) and the back muscles(extensors).

The body will follow the arms so reaching in different directions will help to get a good stretch  but also elongate the body for improved posture.  




Once you feel confident with these exercises please reach out to our head instructor TINA@boxing4health.com and ask to book a meeting time with her to review these exercises and get feedback.

Let's learn VIGOR- here
























































The MUST HAVE’s in every Circuit



V

Voice & Variety

I

Intensity (30-35mins of intensity HR 60-80%) 

G

Grand Movements (Go BIG or Go Home!)

O

Overall Rotation   (Cervical & Thoracic)

R

Release (Myofascial Release)


Voice & Variety- With PD, the students voice can be affected but not everyone experiences this. Their voice can become quite quiet, slow and hard to understand. The more you use it you won’t lose it! 
It’s very important in our classes to add voice exercises in the warm ups and during the circuits. We encourage you to create dialogue with your students during the session. Ie. A very effective warm up is having the class hum as a group and see who can hold their hum the longest, singing, word association, and name games are fun ways to involve vocal elements in your class.
You DON’T want to have them start yelling right at the beginning of class as the VOICE box are muscles too and they need to be warmed up with exercises just like the rest of our body.
Examples of voice exercises to implement into your class. 
1- Humming a short song during your warm up ie. happy birthday 
2- Playing a word game during your warm up or as part of your class. ie. Can you name makes of cars using the alphabet starting with the letter A(audi), B(BMW),C(chevrolet)..... You can moe around the room getting each student to name one. You could also do the same with vegetables or fruits. 
3- Practicing vowel sounds A, E, I, O, U making sure they are getting their whole face involved in  making the sound and trying to make the sound last as long as possible. Always DEMO it for them so they are comfortable dong silly exercises and noises. 


Why HIGH INTENSITY?
High intensity includes aerobic exercise but it also combines the amount of power and output you put into the exercise. If you think about getting out of your comfy couch most of us tend to use adaptations (i.e. using our hands to push us off, using the arm of the couch, or using someone else) or compensatory muscles like the strength of our arms to push us off the couch or chair. What we are lacking is our effort in the POWER and the INTENSITY department to build momentum to get off of the couch!! 
Intense exercise, specifically non-contact boxing classes have proven to reverse, reduce and even delay the symptoms of PD. We aim to get our boxers to work in their 60-80% target heart rate zone during the high intensity portion of the class.
Anyone at any level can lessen their symptoms and lead a healthier and happier life J
Client: “I stay in shape, I walk everyday!”
Walking is something we need to do everyday just to stay alive:) it is definitely NOT enough exercise to help you slow down the progression of PD or many other aging related effects. 
INTENSITY is not NEGOTIABLE!!


Grand Movements- Large amplitude, whole body movements. It’s important to really emphasize everything in class with grand gestures and remind the students that when they try to do this it will get them to ‘normal’.


Overall Rotation- Rigidity is very common in almost everyone with Parkinson’s Disease. It’s common in Seniors as well. They can experience whole body rigidity, but the most prominent area is in the trunk region. This area has the greatest impact on  the student’s ability to rotate. When someone can’t rotate their thoracic spine, this lack of rotation causes the shoulders, hips, knees and back to overcompensate and increases the chance of injury. You should have at least one exercise that targets rotation in the functional exercise circuit and cue rotation in the hips during the boxing stations. 
NOTE: Most students lack self-awareness and when you show them how to rotate, they think they are moving correctly. It’s very helpful if you ask them if you can place your hands on their hips and move them where they need to go and get them to feel the difference. (This often has to happen several times)


Release- Releasing tight fascia improves movement, relieves tightness and overall tension. 
What is fascia? Its bands of connective tissue that stabilizes, encloses and separates muscles and organs. 
We use our cool downs to pick a part of the body to work on with massage balls to help loosen areas of the body that tend to focus on our alignment and posture the most (i.e. the back, chest, feet, shoulders etc.)
A video that shows stretches and releases to give you an idea of what we do in class.

How to set up for class- here









































* Set up your circuits before class. You can use one large board or individual dry erase boards per station

    * Greet students with high energy and motivation when they enter the gym.

    * NEW students NEED to have a liability waiver signed before doing the class. Please be aware of where forms are in the gym.

    * B4H instructors plan or choreograph their own classes. They choose music that is appropriate for their exercise class and create a routine for a class to follow. We use a boxing i timer app located on the IPAD. If you have another app for timing of circuits feel free to use it as well. On Spotify there is a Boxing 4 Health playlist.

    

IMPORTANT: Constantly check “Boxing 4 Health Instructor Forum” for new exercises and cognitive ideas for class.

   * Take attendance, make sure students sign in (It’s a fine motor skill J). A great way to show the students how their symptoms can improve with exercise is to have them sign their name or better yet a motivational quote before class and then have them write it again right after class and there will likely be an improvement.

    * Demonstrate how to carry out various exercises and routines.

   * Watch clients do exercises and show or tell them correct techniques to minimize injury and improve fitness.

    * Demonstrate modifications of exercises for different levels of fitness and skill during explanation of circuits.

    * Monitor clients’ progress and adapt programs as needed.

   * Explain and enforce safety rules, the importance of proper technique, and the use of exercise equipment.

    * We do not expect instructors to handle money from students BUT if for some reason money is left with you please be sure to store it in safe place or leave it in the office for safe keeping and alert Head Instructor or Gym Manager.

How to set up for class- here





















* Set up your circuits before class. You can use one large board or individual dry erase boards per station

* Greet students with high energy and motivation when they enter the gym.

* NEW students NEED to have a liability waiver signed before doing the class. Please be aware of where forms are in the gym.

* B4H instructors plan or choreograph their own classes. They choose music that is appropriate for their exercise class and create a routine for a class to follow. We use a boxing i timer app located on the IPAD. If you have another app for timing of circuits feel free to use it as well. On Spotify there is a Boxing 4 Health playlist.

IMPORTANT: Constantly check “Boxing 4 Health Instructor Forum” for new exercises and cognitive ideas for class.

* Take attendance, make sure students sign in (It’s a fine motor skill J). A great way to show the students how their symptoms can improve with exercise is to have them sign their name or better yet a motivational quote before class and then have them write it again right after class and there will likely be an improvement.

* Demonstrate how to carry out various exercises and routines.

* Watch clients do exercises and show or tell them correct techniques to minimize injury and improve fitness.

* Demonstrate modifications of exercises for different levels of fitness and skill during explanation of circuits.

* Monitor clients’ progress and adapt programs as needed.

* Explain and enforce safety rules, the importance of proper technique, and the use of exercise equipment.

* We do not expect instructors to handle money from students BUT if for some reason money is left with you please be sure to store it in safe place or leave it in the office for safe keeping and alert Head Instructor or Gym Manager.

GO BIG- Big walk around the gym(can be done in rows or a group circle depending on space, High Knees around the gym, Butt Kicks, Monster walk(BIG lateral steps using the arms)

Cueing Students- here











































 

As the cognitive and physical symptoms of Parkinson’s Disease progress, the need for proper cueing will become more and more important. It can be very challenging as an instructor to communicate the important details of your chosen exercises. The three most essential cueing techniques for all levels fall into three categories: Vocal, Mirroring, and Physical Feedback.





Vocal

Using your voice in a clear and direct manner can help cut through the noise and communicate your points clearly and effectively. Embrace repetition, repeating the important points as needed until the message gets across. Your clients will feed off of the energy you bring to class, so take a moment to center yourself and project as much excitement, positivity and confidence as possible :) 

VIDEO


Mirroring

Over and above a simple demonstration, mirroring the movement for your client follow along is a vital tool for helping your most affected clients. Position yourself directly in front of your client and mirror the movements in the largest fashion possible. Seeing exactly what they need to do will bring a sense of calm and comfort, as their trusted instructor guides them through a challenging and beneficial movement.

VIDEO


Physical Feedback

The sense of touch can be used in conjunction with visual and auditory cues to bring the best out of your clients. Remember to always establish consent before putting your hands on a client’s body. As you develop comfort with class participants, consent may become implied. However, it is still necessary to confirm informed consent every time you want to use physical contact as a teaching aid. Something as simple as tapping on a body part can bring enough awareness to encourage your clients to find greater range, ability and balance.

VIDEO

Please make sure to put away equipment used and take your personal equipment items with you when you LOCK up and leave the building.

If you forget your key, there is a drop box on the door please see Office Management for CODE (HQ Ottawa) only.

Newer students need help wrapping their hands (high functioning classes only) so please make sure everyone has their hands wrapped by start of class. Best to use volunteers if they know how.

INCIDENT REPORT: If anyone gets hurt during class please make sure to fill out an incident report ASAP after the class is over and please INFORM management asap. The incident report sheets are in the folder on the office door at HQ or in the communication book (for all other locations).

In the event of an emergency, please be aware of where the emergency plan is in the building.

All instructors are required to have CPR and recertification done every two (2) years.

In the event of an emergency, if you are certified, please provide first aid or CPR if needed (Defibrillator located on Blue gym wall at front of building).

If your gym has a defibrillator please be aware of where it is and how to access it.

Volunteers

They are there to help you run a safe, fun and high energy class!

    Please get them as involved as possible.

    Once they are familiar with your gym have them help with setup and take down of equipment.

    Holding pads (if they are trained to do so). SAFETY is our first priority so please don’t encourage untrained volunteers to hold pads.

    Show them box of cognitive games to go around and use with students during class (flash cards, math cards, etc.)

    Having them work one-on-one with a specific student is TOP priority (client having an off day, client with a DBS, higher fall risk/unstable, cognitive slowness).

    Challenge them to find ways to get students to use their voice more in class.

    Have them run a warm up if they are interested.

    IMPORTANT to review volunteer expectations with family members especially with low functioning as you may need them to help when you are low on staff or volunteers.



Where do we get Volunteers from?

    Retired Seniors who have an interest in giving back and are relatively healthy depending on what class you need them in.

    University / College students: Reach out to university departments that have placement programs (i.e. Kinesiology, Neuroscience, Fitness and Recreation) to see if they need placement opportunities as MOST do!

    High school students: Most HS Students need forty (40) hours of volunteer work but make sure to screen them to see how willing and able they are to work with our population and the importance of their commitment.






Our classes are divided into 4 segments. The segments consist of a Warm Up, Functional Exercises, Boxing, and Cool Down. The goals each of segment is the same for both Fighter (High Functioning) and Champion (Low Functioning) classes. The Fighter classes consist of higher functioning participants and allow more freedom with exercise selection. The Champions classes require more careful exercise selection, more modifications and a slower/more consistent pace. 




This is the volunteer orientation we send to all of our volunteers and ask that they watch it in full before starting with us. It gives them a basic understanding of the population.
